overview:
The Gāyatrī Mantra is one of the most popular Vedic chants. It is a powerful vibration that helps with collective intelligence, and with connecting to the infinite Sun.

`oṁ bhūr bhuva̱s suva̍ḥ |` Pervading the gross, subtle, and the causal

`tat-sa̍vi̱turvare̎ṇya̱m` That life sustaining, resplendent

`bhargo̍ de̱vasya̍ dhīmahi |` divine effulgence, we meditate

**We meditate on THAT divine, life-sustaining, resplendent effulgence, pervading the gross, the subtle and the causal. May THAT supreme intelligence illuminate our intellects.**
structure: The Gayatri has three parts — adoration, meditation, and prayer. First the Divine is praised, then meditated upon in reverence, and finally an appeal is made to awaken and strengthen the intellect, the discriminating faculty of the human being. (Sri Sathya Sai Baba)

quotes.text: The Gayatri is considered the essence of the Vedas. Veda means knowledge, and this prayer fosters and sharpens the knowledge-yielding faculty.
The Gayatri is a universal prayer enshrined in the Vedas. It is addressed to the Immanent and Transcendent Divine, given the name 'Savita' — that from which all this is born.

parallels.text: We pray to You alone and seek help from You alone. Show us the righteous path — the path of those blessed with Your light and grace.
Surrender to Buddha — enlightened awareness. Surrender to Dhamma — inner righteousness. Surrender to Sangha — collective consciousness.
Guide me on the path of righteousness; show me Your way, which is straight, noble and perfect.
Our eyes may see indecent things, but our hearts should be free of impurity. Our ears may hear what is profane, but our hearts should perceive nothing unholy.

**Kuate leno leno mahote** — let me be one with the infinite sun.

**Hayano hayano hayano** — forever, forever, and forever.

Its meaning centres on unity with the infinite sun, to foster spiritual connection and healing. For those who sing it, the power of the chant lies in its communal and meditative resonance, encouraging alignment with the cosmos in general, and specifically with the sun shining forever as a symbol of the inner self.

The spirit of the song is very similar to the Gāyatrī Mantra, which fosters meditation and the collective illumination of our intellects by the divine, life-sustaining, resplendent effulgence of the infinite sun. Tuning into that, we realise that we are not just bodies and minds. We are beyond — as in the forever shining sun.

overview:
May the common people (prajaabhyah - subjects) be governed and nourished by the rulers (pari paalayantaam). Let there be happiness and peace (svasti) for the people.

May those who rule (mahiishaah - king) the land (mahiim), tread the path of justice (nyaayena maargena).

May knowledge (go - cows and rays of knowledge) and the teachers of knowledge (braamhanebhyah) be (astu) ever (nityam) well (shubam).

May (bhavantu) all the worlds (lokha) be happy (sukhino).

Peace to body, mind and soul.

overview: The one who understands the flowers (puṣpam) of the waters (āpaḥ), and their relationship to the moon (candramāḥ), reaches the highest abode. Bhagawan Sri Sathya Sai Baba explains that āpaḥ — the waters of life — is Love. Read this way, the hymn says: the one who understands the inner significance of Love, and its relationship to the mind, reaches the highest abode. This is all there is to know — the one illumined by Love attains the highest abode.

This mantra points the way beyond the confines of religion to universal human experience.

overview:
The occasion was Christmas Eve of 24 December 1977, at the Sathya Sai Mandir in Brindavan, Whitefield, near Bangalore. The assembled audience was a group of students and faculty of Sri Sathya Sai College, along with visiting devotees. It was in the glorious presence of Sri Sathya Sai Baba himself that a great Vedic scholar, Brahmaśrī Ghandikota Subrahmaṇya Śāstri, was inspired to announce the Sri Satya Sāi Gāyatri — the mystic formula devoted to and invoking Sri Satya Sāi.

`oṃ sā̱yī̱śva̱rāya̍ vi̱dmahe̍ ` We know SAI — Same-As-I — as īśvara, the master of the universe

`sa̱tyade̱vāya̍ dhīmahi ।` We meditate on, and retain, this SAI — So-Am-I — as satyadeva, the truth of light within

`ta̱nna̍s sarva̍ḥ praco̱dayā̎t ॥` May His awareness expand to all, in love and service

`|| oṁ śānti̱ś śānti̱ś śānti̍ḥ ||` Oṁ, Peace, Peace, and Peace

structure: This Satya Sāi Gāyatri, like every other Gāyatri mantra, has 24 syllables in three lines of eight. These mantras invoke the particular power of the deity to **know**, to **retain**, and to **expand** the awareness of the one who chants them.
teachingNote:
*Vidmahe* is knowing. *Dhīmahi* is understanding, or retaining. *Pracodayāt* is expansion.

Knowing is the mind, understanding is the intellect, and expansion is the awareness. In that state of awareness and expansion one achieves *mantra siddhi* — or put simply, becomes the mantra itself.

quotes.text: Every Gayatri Mantra has a revealing prophet or Rishi and a presiding deity, Adhishthana Devata, who is the subject of the Mantra. This Mantra is expressed through the inner workings of Sri Sathya Sai through the mind of Brahmaśri Ghandikota Subrahmanya Śāstri in the presence of Sri Sathya Sai Baba. Needless to say that Sri Sathya Sai Baba himself is the presiding deity of this mystic formula or Mantra.

overview: Śiva means positive, auspicious, serene — the one who is not affected by any kind of negativity. Upāsana comes from upa (close) and āsana (sitting): sitting close to Him. Śivopāsana therefore means being rooted in the consciousness and awareness of Shiva. That consciousness is fundamentally the breath of the entire universe; when we breathe in and breathe out Shiva, we are in Śivopāsana.
structure: Holding the liṅgam, twenty-two mantras consecrate and install it. The five faces of the liṅgam are then worshipped in turn: Sadyojāta facing west, Vāmadeva north, Aghora south, Tatpuruṣa east, and Īśāna facing upward.

verses.meaning: All mantras end with an invocation of peace, made for the purpose of averting all evil. It allows one to be at peace with oneself and the universe, to have calmness and concentration. The three repetitions address the three sources of disturbance: ādhyātmika (from within oneself — mind, body, emotions), ādhibhautika (from other living beings) and ādhidaivika (from natural and cosmic forces).

overview: The word kṛmi works on two levels at once, and this dual meaning is the heart of the hymn's relevance. Literally, it was chanted with precise intention toward the elimination of pests, parasites and disease-causing organisms that threatened crops, livestock and human health. Read inwardly, kṛmi represents anything that eats away at our wellbeing from within — the repetitive thought patterns that erode our peace, the jealousy, anger, fear and greed that infect relationships, the toxic habits that quietly consume our health and time, and the disharmony that spreads through a community like a contagion.
teachingNote: When first translated into English these words can sound startling, even violent — germs are 'slain', their chieftains and parents 'annihilated'. In the ancient world, long before microscopes, the seers already understood that the body, the home and the environment could be invaded by unseen harmful forces. They called these kṛmi, and the language of the hymn is the language of driving them out.

overview:
The Sahanā Vavatu śānti mantra originates in the Taittirīya Upaniṣat, part of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda — specifically in the Śīkṣāvalli, chapter 1, section 1. It is traditionally chanted at the beginning of Veda study sessions, to invoke harmony, protection and mutual understanding between the teacher and the student.

`oṃ | sa̱ha nā̍vavatu ।` Let us all — the teacher and the student — be protected together

`sa̱ha nau̍ bhunaktu ।` Let us all be nourished together

`sa̱ha vī̱rya̍ṅkaravāvahai ।` Let us all work together with great vigour

`te̱ja̱svinā̱vadhī̍tamastu̱` Let our studies illumine our intellects

`mā vi̍dviṣā̱vahai̎ ॥` Let there be no discordance, contradiction or hate amongst us

`oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ` Let there be peace, peace, and peace

overview: Every verse follows the same three-part Gāyatrī pattern: we know (vidmahe) one name of the Divine, we meditate (dhīmahi) on another, and we ask that a third impel or illumine us (pracodayāt). Only the names change — Rudra, Danti, Nandi, Ṣaṇmukha, Garuḍa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Narasiṁha, Āditya, Agni, Durgā, and finally Sāyīśvara as Satyadeva, the God of Truth.
structure:
The pattern is the same as the Gāyatrī Mantra itself — adoration, meditation, then the appeal that the intellect be awakened — repeated for each form of the Divine in turn.

The booklet numbers the verses 1 to 12 and then 18; the numbering here follows the booklet exactly.

overview:
The fire in the belly consumes, that is the Brahman. Consuming the Brahman Himself, so that the energy that is produced is the Brahman. That energy that is produced is used to do the work of the Brahman. The material is Brahman, the one who is consuming is Brahman, it is consumed by the Brahman, it is converted into the Brahman, and that energy helps us to do the work of the Brahman.

I am going to take what you have provided, both solid and liquid, and convert that into the life force within you. I will balance the life forces within you, by digesting the four types of food.

verses.devanagari: तस्मा॒दश्वा॑ अजायन्त । ये के चो॑भ॒याद॑तः । गावो॑ ह जज्ञिरे॒ तस्मा᳚त् । तस्मा᳚ज्जा॒ता अ॑जा॒वयः॑ ॥
verses.iast: tasmā̱daśvā̍ | ajāyanta । ye ke co̍bha̱yāda̍taḥ । gāvo̍ ha jajñire̱ tasmā̎t । tasmā̎jjā̱tā | a̍jā̱vaya̍ḥ ॥ 11 ॥

verses.devanagari: यत्पुरु॑षं॒-व्यँ॑दधुः । क॒ति॒था व्य॑कल्पयन्न् । मुख॒-ङ्किम॑स्य॒ कौ बा॒हू । कावू॒रू पादा॑वुच्येते ॥
verses.iast: yatpuru̍ṣa̱ṁu vya̍dadhuḥ । ka̱ti̱dhā vya̍kalpayan । mukha̱ṅ kima̍sya̱ kau bā̱hū । kāvū̱rū pādā̍vucyete ॥ 12 ॥

verses.devanagari: ब्रा॒ह्म॒णो᳚-ऽस्य॒ मुख॑मासीत् । बा॒हू रा॑ज॒न्यः॑ कृ॒तः । ऊ॒रू तद॑स्य॒ यद्वैश्यः॑ । प॒द्भ्याग्ं शू॒द्रो अ॑जायत ॥
verses.iast: brā̱hma̱ṇo̎'sya̱ mukha̍māsīt । bā̱hū rā̍ja̱nya̍ḥ kṛ̱taḥ । ū̱rū tada̍sya̱ yadvaiśya̍ḥ । pa̱dbhyāgṁ śū̱dro | a̍jāyata ॥ 13 ॥

verses.devanagari: च॒न्द्रमा॒ मन॑सो जा॒तः । चक्षो॒-स्सूर्यो॑ अजायत । मुखा॒दिन्द्र॑श्चा॒ग्निश्च॑ । प्रा॒णाद्वा॒युर॑जायत ॥
verses.iast: ca̱ndramā̱ mana̍so jā̱taḥ । cakṣo̱s sūryo̍ | ajāyata । mukhā̱dindra̍ścā̱gniśca̍ । prā̱ṇādvā̱yura̍jāyata ॥ 14 ॥

verses.devanagari: नाभ्या॑ आसीद॒न्तरि॑क्षम् । शी॒र् ष्णो द्यौ-स्सम॑वर्तत । प॒द्भ्या-म्भूमि॒र्दिश॒-श्श्रोत्रा᳚त् । तथा॑ लो॒काग्ं अ॑कल्पयन्न् ॥
verses.iast: nābhyā̍ | āsīda̱ntari̍kṣam । śī̱rṣṇo dyaus sama̍vartata । pa̱dbhyām bhūmi̱rdiśa̱ś śrotrā̎t । tathā̍ lo̱kāgṁ a̍kalpayan ॥ 15 ॥

verses.devanagari: वेदा॒हमे॒त-म्पुरु॑ष-म्म॒हान्तम्᳚ । आ॒दि॒त्यव॑र्ण॒-न्तम॑स॒स्तु पा॒रे । सर्वा॑णि रू॒पाणि॑ वि॒चित्य॒ धीरः॑ । नामा॑नि कृ॒त्वा-ऽभि॒वद॒न्॒, यदा-ऽऽस्ते᳚ ॥
verses.iast: vedā̱hame̱tam puru̍ṣam ma̱hāntam̎ । ā̱di̱tya va̍rṇa̱n tama̍sa̱stu pā̱re । sarvā̍ṇi rū̱pāṇi̍ vi̱citya̱ dhīra̍ḥ । nāmā̍ni kṛ̱tvā'bhi̱vada̱n yadāste̎ ॥ 16 ॥

verses.devanagari: धा॒ता पु॒रस्ता॒द्यमु॑दाज॒हार॑ । श॒क्रः प्रवि॒द्वा-न्प्र॒दिश॒श्चत॑स्रः । तमे॒वं-विँ॒द्वान॒मृत॑ इ॒ह भ॑वति । नान्यः पन्था॒ अय॑नाय विद्यते ॥
verses.iast: dhā̱tā pu̱rastā̱dyamu̍dāja̱hāra̍ । śa̱kraḥ(f) pravi̱dvānpra̱diśa̱ścata̍sraḥ । tame̱vaṁu vi̱dvāna̱mṛta̍ | i̱ha bha̍vati । nānyaḥ(f) panthā̱ | aya̍nāya vidyate ॥ 17 ॥

verses.devanagari: य॒ज्ञेन॑ य॒ज्ञम॑यजन्त दे॒वाः । तानि॒ धर्मा॑णि प्रथ॒मान्या॑सन्न् । ते ह॒ नाक॑-म्महि॒मानः॑ सचन्ते । यत्र॒ पूर्वे॑ सा॒ध्या-स्सन्ति॑ दे॒वाः ॥
verses.iast: ya̱jñena̍ ya̱jñama̍yajanta de̱vāḥ । tāni̱ dharmā̍ṇi pratha̱mānyā̍san । te ha̱ nāka̍ṁ, mahi̱māna̍s sacante । yatra̱ pūrve̍ sā̱dhyās santi̍ de̱vāḥ ॥ 18 ॥

verses.devanagari: अ॒द्भ्य-स्सम्भू॑तः पृथि॒व्यै रसा᳚च्च । वि॒श्वक॑र्मण॒-स्सम॑वर्त॒ताधि॑ । तस्य॒ त्वष्टा॑ वि॒दध॑द्रू॒पमे॑ति । तत्पुरु॑षस्य॒ विश्व॒माजा॑न॒मग्रे᳚ ॥
verses.iast: a̱dbhyas sambhū̍taḥ(f) pṛthi̱vyai rasā̎cca । vi̱śvaka̍rmaṇa̱s sama̍varta̱tādhi̍ । tasya̱ tvaṣṭā̍ vi̱dadha̍drū̱pame̍ti । tatpuru̍ṣasya̱ viśva̱mājā̍na̱magre̎ ॥ 1 ॥

verses.devanagari: वेदा॒हमे॒त-म्पुरु॑ष-म्म॒हान्तम्᳚ । आ॒दि॒त्यव॑र्ण॒-न्तम॑सः॒ पर॑स्तात् । तमे॒वं-विँ॒द्वान॒मृत॑ इ॒ह भ॑वति । नान्यः पन्था॑ विद्य॒ते-ऽय॑नाय ॥
verses.iast: vedā̱hame̱tam puru̍ṣam ma̱hāntam̎ । ā̱di̱tyava̍rṇa̱n tama̍sa̱ḥ(f) para̍stāt । tame̱vaṁu vi̱dvāna̱mṛta̍ | i̱ha bha̍vati । nānyaḥ(f) panthā̍ vidya̱te'ya̍nāya ॥ 2 ॥

verses.devanagari: प्र॒जाप॑तिश्चरति॒ गर्भे॑ अ॒न्तः । अ॒जाय॑मानो बहु॒धा विजा॑यते । तस्य॒ धीराः॒ परि॑जानन्ति॒ योनिम्᳚ । मरी॑चीना-म्प॒दमि॑च्छन्ति वे॒धसः॑ ॥
verses.iast: pra̱jāpa̍tiścarati̱ garbhe̍ | a̱ntaḥ । a̱jāya̍māno bahu̱dhā vijā̍yate । tasya̱ dhīrā̱ḥ(f) pari̍jānanti̱ yonim̎ । marī̍cīnām pa̱dami̍cchanti ve̱dhasa̍ḥ ॥ 3 ॥

verses.devanagari: यो दे॒वेभ्य॒ आत॑पति । यो दे॒वाना᳚-म्पु॒रोहि॑तः । पूर्वो॒ यो दे॒वेभ्यो॑ जा॒तः । नमो॑ रु॒चाय॒ ब्राह्म॑ये ॥
verses.iast: yo de̱vebhya̱ | āta̍pati । yo de̱vānā̎m pu̱rohi̍taḥ । pūrvo̱ yo de̱vebhyo̍ jā̱taḥ । namo̍ ru̱cāya̱ brāhma̍ye ॥ 4 ॥

verses.devanagari: रुच॑-म्ब्रा॒ह्म-ञ्ज॒नय॑न्तः । दे॒वा अग्रे॒ तद॑ब्रुवन्न् । यस्त्वै॒व-म्ब्रा᳚ह्म॒णो वि॒द्यात् । तस्य॑ दे॒वा अस॒न् वशे᳚ ॥
verses.iast: ruca̍m brā̱hmañ ja̱naya̍ntaḥ । de̱vā | agre̱ tada̍bruvan । yastvai̱vam brā̎hma̱ṇo vi̱dyāt । tasya̍ de̱vā | asa̱nvaśe̎ ॥ 5 ॥

verses.devanagari: ह्रीश्च॑ ते ल॒क्ष्मीश्च॒ पत्न्यौ᳚ । अ॒हो॒रा॒त्रे पा॒र् श्वे । नक्ष॑त्राणि रू॒पम् । अ॒श्विनौ॒ व्यात्तम्᳚ । इ॒ष्ट-म्म॑निषाण । अ॒मु-म्म॑निषाण । सर्व॑-म्मनिषाण ॥
verses.iast: hrīśca̍ te la̱kṣmīśca̱ patnyau̎ । a̱ho̱rā̱tre pā̱r·śve । nakṣa̍trāṇi rū̱pam । a̱śvinau̱ vyāttam̎ । i̱ṣṭam ma̍niṣāṇa । a̱mum ma̍niṣāṇa । sarva̍m maniṣāṇa ॥ 6 ॥

verses.devanagari: तच्छं॒-योँरावृ॑णीमहे । गा॒तुं-यँ॒ज्ञाय॑ । गा॒तुं-यँ॒ज्ञप॑तये । दैवी᳚ स्व॒स्तिर॑स्तु नः । स्व॒स्तिर्मानु॑षेभ्यः । ऊ॒र्ध्व-ञ्जि॑गातु भेष॒जम् । श-न्नो॑ अस्तु द्वि॒पदे᳚ । श-ञ्चतु॑ष्पदे ।
verses.iast: oṁ | tacha̱ṁi yorāvṛ̍ṇīmahe । gā̱tuṁi ya̱jñāya̍ । gā̱tuṁi ya̱jña pa̍taye । daivī̎ sva̱stira̍stu naḥ । sva̱stir mānu̍ṣebhyaḥ । ū̱rdhvañ ji̍gātu bheṣa̱jam । śan no̍ | astu dvi̱pade̎ । śañ catu̍ṣpade ॥

verses.devanagari: ॐ शान्ति॒-श्शान्ति॒-श्शान्तिः॑ ॥
verses.iast: oṁ | śāntiś śāntiś śānti̍ḥ ॥

overview: The Puruṣa Sūktam describes the Cosmic Person — thousand-headed, thousand-eyed, thousand-footed — who pervades the earth entirely and extends beyond it. It sets out creation as a yajña in which the Puruṣa is at once the offering, the fire and the one to whom it is offered, and from which the Vedas, the creatures, the elements and the worlds all arise.
structure: Two anuvākas. The first has eighteen verses, the second six. Both are framed by the same śānti — śaṁ yorāvṛṇīmahe — which opens the recitation and closes it again as the samāptāśīrvācanam.

note: Salutation to Rudra in every form and in every place, and then the asking. Chanted for peace within and without.

sections.label: Namakam
sections.note: Taittirīya Saṃhitā, fourth kāṇḍa, fifth prapāṭhaka.

verses.iast: ॥ oṁ | namo bhagavate̍ rudrā̱ya ॥
oṁ | nama̍ste rudra ma̱nyava̍ | u̱tota̱ | iṣa̍ve̱ nama̍ḥ । nama̍ste | astu̱ dhanva̍ne bā̱hubhyā̍mu̱ta te̱ nama̍ḥ
yā ta̱ | iṣu̍ś śi̱vata̍mā śi̱vam ba̱bhūva̍ te̱ dhanu̍ḥ । śi̱vā śa̍ra̱vyā̍ yā tava̱ tayā̍ no rudra mṛḍaya
yā te̍ rudra śi̱vā ta̱nūragho̱rā'pā̍pakāśinī । tayā̍ nasta̱nuvā̱ śanta̍mayā̱ giri̍śantā̱bhi cā̍kaśīḥ
yāmiṣu̍ṅ giriśanta̱ haste̱ bibha̱rṣyasta̍ve । śi̱vāṅ gi̍ritra̱ tāṅ ku̍ru̱ mā hi̍gṁsī̱ḥ(f) puru̍ṣa̱ñ jaga̍t
śi̱vena̱ vaca̍sā tvā̱ giri̱śācchā̍ vadāmasi । yathā̍ na̱s sarva̱mijjaga̍daya̱kṣmagṁ su̱manā̱ | asa̍t
adhya̍vocadadhiva̱ktā pra̍tha̱mo daivyo̍ bhi̱ṣak । ahī̍gśca̱ sarvā̎ñ ja̱mbhaya̱nth sarvā̎śca yātu dhā̱nya̍ḥ
a̱sau yastā̱mro | a̍ru̱ṇa | u̱ta ba̱bhrus su̍ma̱ṅgala̍ḥ । ye ce̱māgṁ ru̱drā | a̱bhito̍ di̱kṣu śri̱tās sa̍hasra̱śo'vai̍ṣā̱gṁ heḍa̍ | īmahe
a̱sau yo̍'va̱sarpa̍ti̱ nīla̍grīvo̱ vilo̍hitaḥ । u̱taina̍ṅ go̱pā | a̍dṛśa̱nnadṛ̍śannudahā̱rya̍ḥ । u̱taina̱ṁu viśvā̍ bhū̱tāni̱ sa dṛ̱ṣṭo mṛ̍ḍayāti naḥ
namo̍ | astu̱ nīla̍grīvāya sahasrā̱kṣāya̍ mī̱ḍhuṣe̎ । atho̱ ye | a̍sya̱ satvā̍no̱'han tebhyo̍'kara̱n nama̍ḥ
pramu̍ñca̱ dhanva̍na̱stvamu̱bhayo̱rārtni̍yo̱rjyām । yāśca̍ te̱ hasta̱ | iṣa̍va̱ḥ(f) parā̱ tā bha̍gavo vapa
a̱va̱tatya̱ dhanu̱stvagṁ saha̍srākṣa̱ śate̍ṣudhe । ni̱śīrya̍ śa̱lyānā̱m mukhā̍ śi̱vo na̍s su̱manā̍ bhava
vijya̱n dhanu̍ḥ kapa̱rdino̱ viśa̍lyo̱ bāṇa̍vāgṁ u̱ta । ane̍śanna̱syeṣa̍va | ā̱bhura̍sya niṣa̱ṅgathi̍ḥ
yā te̍ he̱tirmī̍ḍhuṣṭama̱ haste̍ ba̱bhūva̍ te̱ dhanu̍ḥ । tayā̱'smān vi̱śvata̱stvama̍ya̱kṣmayā̱ pari̍bbhuja
nama̍ste | a̱stvāyu̍dhā̱yānā̍tatāya dhṛ̱ṣṇave̎ । u̱bhābhyā̍mu̱ta te̱ namo̍ bā̱hubhyā̱n tava̱ dhanva̍ne
pari̍ te̱ dhanva̍no he̱tira̱smān vṛ̍ṇaktu vi̱śvata̍ḥ । atho̱ ya | i̍ṣu̱dhistavā̱re | a̱smannidhe̍hi̱ tam
॥ śambhave̱ nama̍ḥ ॥

overview: Śrī Rudram is the central hymn to Rudra in the Kṛṣṇa Yajur Veda. Its first half, the Namakam, is named for the word namaḥ — salutations — which recurs throughout as Rudra is saluted in every form and in every place. Its second half, the Chamakam, is named for the phrase ca me — and for me — in which each verse asks that some good be granted.
structure: Eleven anuvākas in each half, chanted in sequence. Classes usually work through one anuvāka at a time, which is how the anuvākas are presented here.

overview:
A hymn to Durgā as the fire that carries one across difficulty. *Durgāṇi* means hard places or straits, and the refrain asks Agni — *jātavedas*, knower of all that is born — to ferry us over them as a boat carries one over a river. It closes with the Kātyāyanī Gāyatrī.

Read more deeply, the Sūktam describes the journey of a **perfect instrument of God** — a path exemplified by Moses — in which one must move beyond personal desires and sacrifice the self for the **mass consciousness**.

figureParallel.heading: The Sūktam and the life of Moses
figureParallel.intro: The Durgā Sūktam has been called the **essence of the life of Moses**. Though its mantras are thousands of years old, they are held to be eternally relevant to the lives of all Messiahs. The relationship is drawn through six thematic and narrative parallels.

items.title: The vision of fire on Mount Sinai
items.text: When Moses ascended Mount Sinai he encountered a pillar of fire — the same *Agni*, the fire aspect, that the Sūktam worships. Just as the Sūktam invokes the god of fire to purify intent and instinct, Moses encountered the Divine as light and fire.

items.title: The prayer for liberation and prosperity
items.text: Moses prayed for his people to be liberated from slavery and for his clan to prosper. The Sūktam mirrors this: a plea to the fire of God to help the clan cross obstacles, and to ensure abundance on Mother Earth and auspiciousness for all children and spouses.

items.title: Crossing the Red Sea
items.text: The Sūktam prays to cross the ocean of this life, using surrender to God as the boat. This links directly to the parting of the Red Sea. The mantra *vishanava* is read as a call for the Lord of Light to take the people across the sea, escaping the pursuing enemies of the Pharaoh's army.

items.title: Victory over enemies
items.text: Moses fleeing the Egyptian army corresponds to the Sūktam's invocation to defeat all enemies that obstruct one from doing God's work — a supreme consciousness called upon to destroy obstacles both outward, like the Pharaoh, and inward, like bad qualities or laziness.

items.title: The connection to Atri Maharishi
items.text: Atri Maharishi has been described as another Moses within Hinduism. The Sūktam speaks of being **like Atri** — having no attachment, and a singular focus on praying for the happiness and peace of all creation.

items.title: The Ten Commandments as obstacles
items.text: The Ten Commandments correspond to the common-sense obstacles the Sūktam helps devotees overcome. These are the lower-level obstacles — stealing, adultery, things human beings do knowingly — which the fire of the Sūktam seeks to purify.

overview:
A hymn addressed to **Medhā**, the faculty of intelligence itself, personified as a goddess. The chanter does not ask to be given knowledge but to be made *fit to hold it*: a body that does not tire, a tongue that speaks sweetly, ears that hear widely, and a mind that keeps what it has received.

The refrain *mayi medhāṁ mayi prajāṁ* — "in me intelligence, in me progeny" — asks Agni, Indra and Sūrya each to place their own quality within the one chanting. It closes with the Haṁsa Gāyatrī.

title.english: The Thousand Names of the Divine Mother

note: A thousand names of the Divine Mother, sung one after another — each name another way of naming the same Presence.
overview:
The Lalitā Sahasranāma is a litany of names. It opens with a *dhyāna* verse — a picture of the Mother held in the mind before a word is chanted — and then gives a thousand names of her across a hundred and eighty-three stanzas, closing as it began, with her name alone.

Each name is a description rather than a label: the Mother as the Great Empress, as the fire of pure consciousness, as the one whose form is the union of Śiva and Śakti. Taken together they say that no single name is sufficient, and that is the teaching the chant carries — the same Presence seen from a thousand directions.
structure: Dhyānam, then the names in nineteen groups of ten stanzas, then the close. A group is about a minute and a half, which is as much as most students take on at one sitting.
